description: YAML.JSX is a high-octane engineering crew from UNITBV encapsulating the full spectrum of tech evolution. We connect the fresh creativity of Bogdan Diaconiță (1st Yr CE) and sharp drive of Cezar Sava (2nd Yr CE) with the battle-tested development architecture of Ștefania Roman and Adelin Olteanu (3rd Yr CE). The matrix is anchored by Valentin Floricescu, an Applied Electronics alumnus and PhD researcher. From freshman spark to doctoral depth, we deliver flawless execution.
summary: Fire Pattern Predictor turns raw NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections into tracked fires and a calibrated three-day forecast for every active fire, shown on an interactive 3D globe. MODIS, VIIRS and Landsat report the same fire many times, at different resolutions, and miss it under clouds. Our pipeline harmonises the sensors, links detections into fires and measures each fire's position, spread, radiative power, starting point and pass-by-pass expansion: ignitions, merges, splits and extinctions. Hourly Open-Meteo weather is attached and every result goes into a Neo4j knowledge graph: 18.7 million nodes for 2,000 fires from ten years of data, so every prediction traces back to its satellite pixels. Linking fires hidden by clouds into chains fixed false extinctions. GPU-trained XGBoost survival and growth models, blended with a recurrent neural network and using terrain and land cover, predict each fire's growth, direction, fire power, chance of going out or merging, and a 1 km burn-chance map for the next three days. In the app, users pick a country or draw a zone, run the pipeline stage by stage and explore the forecast, fire cards and weather layers. Tested on 2025-2026 data they never saw, extinction chances are calibrated within two points, and an end-to-end backtest called 68.6% of fire outcomes right, against 38.8% for assuming every fire keeps burning.
details:
Wildfire agencies receive thousands of NASA satellite fire detections every day. Those detections are points, not fires. They say nothing about which detections belong together, how a fire started, or what it will do tomorrow. Fire Pattern Predictor closes that gap with three parts: a tracking pipeline, a knowledge graph and an AI forecast, all shown in one web app.

Data. We use the NASA FIRMS API for MODIS, VIIRS and Landsat detections, near real time plus a ten-year archive (2016–2026). Weather comes from Open-Meteo: ERA5 observations, archived ECMWF forecasts and the live forecast. Terrain comes from the Copernicus DEM and land cover from ESA WorldCover, both from AWS open data.

Harmonisation. The sensors differ in pixel size (30 m to 5 km), detection limit, confidence scale and overpass time. We put them on a common grid with a common minimum fire size. We also reconstruct each satellite's ground track from its own detections, so the system knows when a satellite looked and saw nothing.

Workers. A correlation layer measures how the data fields relate and links detections whose pixels touch. An interpreter routes fields and rows to the workers. Localisation and fire-power workers compute position, extent, spread direction and rate, radiative power, intensity trend, energy and biomass burned. An epicenter worker estimates where and when each fire started. An expansion worker replays every satellite pass and records ignitions, new bursts, merges, splits and extinctions. A weather worker attaches hourly weather and measures fire–weather relationships.

Knowledge graph. Two feeds write every result into one Neo4j graph. The fire feed covers detections, passes, satellites, fires, epicenters, clusters and timeline states. The weather feed covers weather cells and hours, linked to each observation. Every prediction can be traced back to its pixels.

AI prediction. Ten years of FIRMS data gave us 2,000 representative fires and 333,452 fire-days. We found that 43% of apparent extinctions were really fires hidden by clouds or missed passes that reappeared within days. We fixed this by linking those fires into chains and by training a survival model that handles censored data. Production blends GPU-trained XGBoost models with a recurrent neural network (a GRU). Training adds real weather-forecast errors, so the models do not over-trust forecasts. For each of the next three days, each fire gets low, likely and high values for growth, movement and fire power, plus chances of growing, going out and merging. A logistic spread map gives a burn chance for every 1 km cell. Version 4 adds slope, uphill wind and fuel type.

Results. On held-out 2025–2026 data, extinction ROC AUC is 0.83–0.86, calibrated within 1–2 points. Merge AUC is 0.93–0.95. The model is about twice as accurate as persistence on direction and growth class. An end-to-end backtest got 68.6% of fire outcomes right, against 38.8% for the baseline.

Frontend. A React and MapLibre 3D globe lets users pick a country or draw a zone, load harmonised detections and run the pipeline stage by stage. They can then explore the forecast, the burn-chance heatmap, fire cards and weather layers.
